blurb: Data, tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism — and keeping a huge training run alive.

cards.title: Same model, different data

steps.p: Every GPU holds a full copy of the model.
Each GPU processes a different slice of the training batch and computes its own gradients.
An all-reduce averages gradients across GPUs, and every copy applies the identical update.

cards.aside: It is the simplest form of parallelism, and almost every run uses it in some form.

cards.q: What is the main limitation of pure data parallelism?
options: The entire model, gradients and optimizer state must fit on every GPU
cards.why: Memory. Every GPU holds everything. Once a model's training state exceeds one GPU's memory, you need to split the model itself.

cards.q: Training with Adam in mixed precision needs about 16 bytes per parameter before activations. Roughly how much memory does a 7B model need?
cards.why: About 112 GB. 2 bytes for BF16 weights, 2 for gradients, and 12 for the FP32 master weights and Adam's two moment estimates. That is more than one 80 GB GPU.

cards.statement: Data parallelism produces the same result as training on one giant GPU with the full batch.
cards.why: True, mathematically. Averaging gradients from slices equals the full-batch gradient. Only floating-point rounding order differs.

cards.title: Microsoft's ZeRO technique removed the redundant copies that data parallelism wastes memory on.
cards.detail: Introduced in 2019 in DeepSpeed, ZeRO shards optimizer states, gradients and even parameters across GPUs, fetching pieces only when needed. PyTorch's FSDP follows the same idea.

cards.q: Fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP or ZeRO-3) saves memory by…
options: Splitting parameters, gradients and optimizer state across GPUs instead of replicating them
cards.why: Sharding. Each GPU stores a fraction and gathers the rest just in time, trading extra communication for much less memory per GPU.

cards.title: Tensor and pipeline parallelism

steps.p: Individual matrix multiplications are split across GPUs — each computes part of every layer. This needs very fast, frequent communication.
Layers are divided into stages on different GPUs, like an assembly line. Data passes stage to stage.
Splitting each batch into small microbatches keeps more stages busy at once.

cards.aside: Large runs combine data, tensor and pipeline parallelism — often called 3D parallelism.

cards.q: Why is tensor parallelism usually kept within a single server?
options: It needs extremely frequent, high-bandwidth communication that only links like NVLink provide
It only works on 8 GPUs exactly
cards.why: Bandwidth. Tensor-parallel GPUs exchange data inside every layer. Over slower links between servers, they would spend most of their time waiting.

options: Idle time when pipeline stages wait for work at the start and end of a batch
cards.why: Idle stages. The first stage starts before later ones have work, and the last finishes after the first is done. More microbatches shrink the bubble.

cards.statement: Pipeline parallelism needs less communication bandwidth than tensor parallelism.
cards.why: True. Pipeline stages only pass activations between neighbors once per microbatch, so they can span slower links between servers.

cards.title: Meta trained Llama 3 405B using four kinds of parallelism at once.
cards.detail: On about 16,000 H100s it combined tensor, pipeline, context and data parallelism — splitting layers, matrices, long sequences and batches simultaneously.

cards.statement: NVIDIA's Megatron-LM work helped popularize tensor parallelism for transformers.
cards.why: True. The 2019 Megatron-LM paper showed how to split attention and MLP layers across GPUs with only a few communication steps per layer.

cards.title: More ways to split

steps.p: In mixture-of-experts models, different experts live on different GPUs, and tokens are sent to whichever GPU holds their chosen expert.
Routing tokens means every GPU sends data to every other one, twice per MoE layer.
Very long sequences are split across GPUs, which pass keys and values around in turn so each sees the whole context.

cards.aside: Each new axis of parallelism trades memory or compute for communication.

cards.q: Expert parallelism relies heavily on which communication pattern?
cards.why: All-to-all. Each GPU dispatches tokens to the GPUs hosting the selected experts, then collects results back — a demanding pattern for the network.

cards.statement: Ring attention lets attention over a very long sequence be split across many GPUs.
cards.why: True. Each GPU holds one block of the sequence and passes key-value blocks around a ring, overlapping communication with computation.

cards.q: Why do MoE models add a load-balancing loss during training?
options: To stop the router sending most tokens to a few experts while others sit idle
cards.why: Even usage. Without it, routers often collapse onto a few favorite experts, overloading their GPUs and wasting the rest.

cards.title: DeepSeek wrote custom low-level GPU code to work around export-restricted chips.
cards.detail: Its H800 GPUs had reduced chip-to-chip bandwidth. The V3 report describes custom communication kernels and a "DualPipe" schedule that overlaps nearly all communication with computation.

cards.q: Why do training systems try to overlap communication with computation?
options: So GPUs keep computing while data transfers happen, instead of waiting
cards.why: Hiding latency. If the next transfer runs while the current computation does, communication time effectively disappears.

cards.title: Failure is normal

steps.p: With tens of thousands of GPUs, cables, memory and power supplies, failures happen every few hours.
The full training state is saved regularly, so a crash costs minutes or hours rather than weeks.
Some hardware faults produce wrong numbers without crashing, which can quietly corrupt a run.

cards.aside: At this scale, reliability engineering decides how much of the cluster's time is real progress.

options: Faulty hardware returns wrong results without raising any error
cards.why: No alarm. A chip that miscalculates occasionally may only show up as an odd loss spike, or not at all. Teams detect it with redundant checks and by monitoring statistics.

cards.statement: On a cluster of tens of thousands of GPUs, an interruption every few hours is normal.
cards.why: True. Meta's Llama 3 run on about 16,000 GPUs averaged an interruption roughly every three hours. Bigger clusters fail more often.

cards.q: Why do large runs save checkpoints asynchronously?
options: Writing hundreds of gigabytes would otherwise pause training
cards.why: Avoiding stalls. Copying state to memory quickly and writing it to storage in the background keeps GPUs training.

cards.title: Google trained Gemini Ultra across multiple data centers at once.
cards.detail: Its 2023 technical report describes TPU pods in several facilities working on one run, linked by Google's network — an early example of multi-site training.

cards.title: Estimate training time
cards.body: Time ≈ total FLOPs ÷ (GPUs × peak FLOP/s × utilization). An H100 offers about 10¹⁵ BF16 FLOP/s, and 40% utilization is a good real-world figure.
cards.challenge: How long would 4.2 × 10²² FLOPs take on 1,000 H100s at 40% utilization? (About 29 hours.)
